doc.title: Joe Segal — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
title: Starting the Roosevelt jazz club sessions
summary: He explains how the student jazz club turned into bebop sessions with Ira Sullivan, Richard Davis, Sun Ra's men and a Memphis band including George Coleman.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: I just think - going back once again - that Roosevelt University, and of course... was it Edward Sparling.... The curriculum as it was stated was based upon social justice, and so it seems to me there was a - he was a real pioneer of challenging the time.
Yeah well there was all kinds of clubs there. I think CORE originated there, the Committee of Racial Equality.

And there was a communist club I believe, all kind of clubs. And someone founded the jazz club, but what they did mostly was just listen to records and discuss them. So when I come in I saw these musicians walking around, and said, “let’s have a session,” and it got very popular. It was originally supposed to be a dance.

Put on by the student council. But the music was so challenging and interesting then, that was when bebop was coming up, and the kids found it so interesting. The music of Monk and Charlie Parker, Dizzy, and so forth. They pulled their chairs up to the stage and sat down, and made a concert out of it. All these young people came in that later became famous, like Ira Sullivan who’s still with us, Richard Davis, Andrew Hill...

Yes, yes. Sun Ra used to come up with his guys, John Gilmore and all. And I remember one year we had a set going with Ira and Nicky Hill, they were burnin’ up. And in walks this group from Memphis: George Coleman, Booker Little, Frank Strozier, Harold Mabern, and they had Bob Cranshaw on bass and Walter Perkins on drums, and

they proceeded to burn the place down. And I remember George had on a big Army overcoat, it must have been in the winter, and an open pair of galoshes. He didn’t take them off, he just opened up the sax case, took out the horn, and they start playing. And it was just fantastic.
Wow, wow. So the Jazz Club. Ok, so it really was just a listening club. That’s why it started.
Yeah, that’s what it turned out to be.
And so you saw an opportunity here to expand it, extend it beyond a listening club here.
